questions.prompt: Explain the working of a Convolutional Neural Network.
questions.semanticPrecision: Strict Semantic (Cos-sim cutoff: 0.84 / Concept checks active)
questions.knowledgeCorpus: Goodfellow Ch. 9 & CS231n Syllabus Benchmark Index: Rev 2024.1
questions.expectedAnswer:
A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a deep learning architecture specially tailored for handling data with a grid topology, such as 2D images. Inspired by biological vision mechanisms discovered in animal visual cortices, CNNs achieve parameter efficiency through shared spatial kernels.

The core operation is convolution, where learnable filters slide across an input image with a specified stride, taking element-wise dot products to produce 2D activation maps or feature maps. The output dimension is O = floor((W - F + 2P)/S) + 1.

Next, non-linear activation functions (most commonly ReLU, f(x) = max(0, x)) must be applied to introduce non-linearity and prevent multiple linear layers from collapsing into a single linear map.

To compress the spatial dimensionality, pooling layers (most commonly Max Pooling) downsample the feature representations, introducing translation invariance and reducing compute.

Finally, the multidimensional tensor is flattened into a 1D feature vector and passed through Fully Connected (Dense) layers with Softmax activation for categorical probability estimation. CNNs are widely deployed in autonomous driving pipelines and radiology imaging diagnostics.
keyConcepts: Element-wise dot product and feature maps
Real-world vision applications (medical imaging, autonomous driving)

Articulate why non-linear activation functions prevent linear collapse

questions.knowledgeCorpus: Vaswani et al. (2017) Attention Is All You Need
questions.expectedAnswer: Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes attention weights by taking the inner product of queries Q and keys K, scaled by sqrt(d_k) to prevent vanishing gradients in the Softmax function: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V.

courseDocuments.title: Deep Learning Book - Chapter 9: Convolutional Networks
courseDocuments.subject: Computer Science
courseDocuments.content:
Chapter 9: Convolutional Networks. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a specialized kind of neural network for processing data that has a known, grid-like topology. Examples include time-series data (1D grid) and image data (2D grid of pixels).
Convolution leverages three important ideas: sparse interactions, parameter sharing, and equivariant representations.
In traditional neural networks, matrix multiplication involves every output unit interacting with every input unit. In a CNN, kernels are much smaller than the input image, so connections are sparse.
Parameter sharing means the same kernel is used at every position of the input. This drastically reduces memory requirements.
Equivariance to translation: if we translate the input image, the representation changes in the same way.
Pooling functions replace the output of the net at a certain location with a summary statistic of the nearby outputs, for example Max Pooling. Max pooling reports the maximum output within a rectangular neighborhood.
Non-linear activation functions such as the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU: f(x) = max(0, x)) are essential between linear convolution stages to prevent recursive linear transformations from collapsing into a single linear map.
The output spatial dimension of a convolution stage is O = floor((W - F + 2P)/S) + 1.

courseDocuments.title: Stanford CS231n Lecture 5: Convolutional Neural Networks
courseDocuments.subject: Computer Vision
courseDocuments.content:
CS231n Lecture 5: Convolutional Neural Networks.
Input: 32x32x3 image.
Filters: 5x5x3 filter slides over spatial locations with stride S. Dot product between filter and input chunk plus bias.
Activation Maps: Stack of 2D slices.
Conv Layer preserves spatial structure.
ReLU layer applies elementwise activation max(0,x).
Pooling Layer makes the representations smaller and more manageable, operates over each activation map independently.
Common settings for pooling: 2x2 max pooling with stride 2.
Fully Connected Layer takes all activations and computes class scores. Output dimension is 1xK where K is number of classes.
